title: Synonyms and Antonyms
shortDescription: Same-meaning and opposite-meaning words, taught through context and shades of meaning rather than a raw word list to cram.
genZNote: Two words can mean 'almost' the same thing and still get you the wrong answer if you ignore the shade of meaning.

sections.heading: Why exams test more than 'word = word'
sections.body: A synonym question rarely tests a pure one-to-one match — it tests which option fits the CONTEXT and CONNOTATION (positive/negative/neutral feeling) of the original word. 'Thin' can be replaced by 'slim' (positive connotation) or 'skinny' (often negative) — picking the wrong shade can be marked wrong even though both are technically synonyms.

sections.heading: Connotation: same core meaning, different shade
How to approach antonym questions
bullets: First fix the exact SENSE of the word being used — 'grave' as an adjective (serious) has a different antonym (trivial) than 'grave' as a noun (burial place, no common antonym).

Watch for prefix-based antonyms as a trap: adding un-/in-/dis- to the given word is sometimes offered as a wrong option when a completely different root word is the better, more natural antonym (e.g. antonym of 'ancient' is better given as 'modern' than as an invented 'unancient').
Some words have more than one valid antonym depending on which meaning is intended — always match the antonym to the SAME sense used in the question.

sections.heading: Common negative prefixes for building antonyms
Frequently tested synonym/antonym roots (learn as families, not single words)
bullets: Learning words as PAIRS or small FAMILIES like this is far more exam-efficient than memorising isolated words.

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: Synonym and antonym questions test not just similar/opposite meaning but the correct connotation and sense of the word as used in context.
keyFacts: Connotation (positive/negative/neutral feel) can make a technically-correct synonym the wrong exam answer.
Fix the exact sense/part of speech of the word first, since some words have multiple unrelated meanings.
Negative prefixes (un-, in-, im-, dis-, ir-, il-, mis-, non-) are a fast way to recognise/build antonyms.

highYieldFacts: 'Frugal' has a neutral/positive core meaning but shades toward 'stingy' only with strong negative framing.
Building antonyms by adding a negative prefix isn't always the best answer — a distinct root word is often more natural.
commonTraps: Choosing a synonym with the right core meaning but the wrong emotional shade.
Ignoring that a word has multiple senses and picking an antonym for the wrong one.
mustRemember: Read the sentence context (if given) before choosing between two close synonym options.
possibleQuestions: Choose the word closest in meaning to 'meticulous'.
Choose the antonym of 'abundant' as used in: 'The region has abundant rainfall.'
